briefs.learning_objective: Create and reassign variables to store values using the assignment operator.

required_facts.statement: Assignment binds or rebinds a name to the value of the expression on the right of =.
Use name = value to assign a value, and use the name in a later right-hand expression to reuse its current value.
Names are case-sensitive; ASCII names can contain letters, underscores and digits, but cannot start with a digit or be a keyword.
A right-hand expression can combine named numeric values using +, -, * or / before assigning the result.

briefs.learning_objective: Recognize and use Python's core scalar data types: int, float, str, and bool.

required_facts.statement: An int represents an integer; a numeric literal with a decimal point or exponent produces a float.
Mixed int and float arithmetic converts the int operand to float.
A str represents text and can be created with single- or double-quoted literals; + concatenates strings.
A bool has the values True and False and represents truth values.
Numeric values can be compared for equality or ordering, producing a boolean.
type(value) returns the value’s type.
print(value) displays a string representation of the value.

briefs.learning_objective: Use Python arithmetic operators for numeric calculations.

required_facts.statement: For numeric values, x + y adds, x - y subtracts, x * y multiplies and x / y divides; division of ints produces a float.
x // y gives the floored quotient, x % y gives the remainder and x ** y raises x to power y.
Parentheses group a calculation; exponentiation has higher precedence than multiplication, division and remainder, which have higher precedence than addition and subtraction.

briefs.learning_objective: Compare Python values and produce booleans.

required_facts.statement: x == y tests equality and x != y tests inequality.
x < y and x > y test strict ordering, while x <= y and x >= y include equality.
Comparisons between supported scalar values produce True or False.

briefs.learning_objective: Combine boolean conditions with and, or, and not.

required_facts.statement: For boolean conditions, a and b is true when both are true; a or b is true when at least one is true; not a reverses its truth value.
and skips its second operand when the first is false, while or skips its second operand when the first is true.
not has higher priority than and, which has higher priority than or; parentheses can make the intended grouping explicit.

briefs.learning_objective: Convert a value from one core type to another using casting functions like int(), float(), str().

required_facts.statement: int(value) constructs an integer from suitable numeric text or a number; conversion from float truncates toward zero.
float(text) constructs a floating-point value from text in a supported numeric form.
str(value) constructs a string representation of a value.
An invalid numeric string can raise ValueError, indicating that the value is unsuitable for the requested conversion.
To reuse a converted value in a calculation, assign the conversion result to a name; this does not rebind the original name unless that name is the assignment target.

briefs.learning_objective: Branch program execution based on conditions using if/elif/else.

required_facts.statement: Write if condition: followed by an indented body, with aligned elif condition: bodies and an optional else: body.
Conditions are tested in order and the first true condition’s body executes; else executes if no condition is true.

briefs.learning_objective: Repeat a block of code until a condition becomes false using a while loop.

required_facts.statement: Write while condition: followed by an indented body; the condition is tested before each repetition and the loop stops when it is false.
A false initial condition means the body does not run.
Update the values used by the condition in the loop body so that a condition-based loop can reach its stopping condition.
input(prompt) displays the prompt and returns the entered line as text, excluding its trailing newline; assign its result again in the loop to obtain a new response.

briefs.learning_objective: Create and manipulate Python's core ordered, mutable data structure: the list.

required_facts.statement: Create a list with [item1, item2, ...]; it is an ordered collection that can be changed.
items[0] selects the first item, and negative indices count from the end.
items[start:stop] returns a new list containing items from start up to but not including stop.
items[index] = value replaces an item.
items.append(value) adds a value at the end of the list.

briefs.learning_objective: Create and use Python's core unordered, unique-element data structure: the set.

required_facts.statement: A set is an unordered collection of distinct elements; set(items) constructs one and removes repeated values.
Use {item1, item2, ...} for a nonempty set and set() for an empty set; {} creates a dictionary.
value in values tests set membership.
a | b is union, containing elements in either set; a & b is intersection, containing elements in both sets.

briefs.learning_objective: Create and use Python's core key-value data structure: the dictionary.

required_facts.statement: A dictionary stores key-value pairs with unique keys; use {key: value, ...} to create one.
mapping[key] retrieves the associated value and raises an error if the key is absent.
mapping[key] = value adds a key-value pair or replaces the value for an existing key.

briefs.learning_objective: Create string literals and format values into readable strings using f-strings.

required_facts.statement: Strings represent text, and single or double quotes delimit string literals.
Prefix a string literal with f and place expressions inside braces to insert their values: f"{expression}".
A format specification after a colon controls presentation; f"{value:.2f}" displays a number in fixed-point form with two digits after the decimal point.

briefs.learning_objective: Define a Python function and call it by name.

required_facts.statement: Define a function with def name(): followed by an indented body.
A function definition binds its name to a function; name() calls it and executes its body.

briefs.learning_objective: Pass values into functions through parameters and arguments.

required_facts.statement: Parameters are names listed in a function definition; arguments are the values supplied at a call.
Define def name(parameter): with an indented body using parameter, then call name(argument) to supply that value.
Positional arguments bind to the corresponding parameters in order.

briefs.learning_objective: Return a computed value from a function for later reuse.

required_facts.statement: return expression ends the current function call and supplies that expression’s value to the caller.
Use result = function(arguments) to store a returned value.
A function that reaches its end without return, or uses return without an expression, returns None.
print displays values rather than supplying them as the function’s calculated return result.

briefs.learning_objective: Create and use Python's core ordered, immutable data structure: the tuple.

required_facts.statement: A tuple is an ordered group of values whose individual items cannot be reassigned.
Comma-separated values form a tuple; (value,) creates a one-item tuple.
Unpack a pair with first, second = pair; the number of targets must match the number of values.
return first, second returns a tuple containing the two expression values.
min(values) and max(values) obtain the smallest and largest items of a nonempty collection.

briefs.learning_objective: Give function parameters default values and call functions using keyword argument syntax.

required_facts.statement: Define a default with def name(required, optional=default):; omitting optional in a call uses its default value.
Positional arguments bind in order and keyword arguments bind by parameter name; keyword arguments follow ordinary positional arguments.
A call must supply required arguments and must not bind one parameter twice or supply an unaccepted keyword.

briefs.learning_objective: Understand how local and global scope determine where a variable name is visible and modifiable.

required_facts.statement: A function’s assigned names are local throughout that function unless declared otherwise; reading a local name before binding it raises UnboundLocalError.
Without a local binding, ordinary lookup can read an enclosing or module-level binding.
globals() returns the current module namespace dictionary; globals()["name"] explicitly reads its entry even when an ordinary local name shadows it.
Assigning to an ordinary local name changes that local binding rather than a same-named module binding.
A global declaration makes assignments to the declared name use its module-level binding instead.

briefs.learning_objective: Catch and handle runtime errors gracefully using try/except.

required_facts.statement: Wrap the operation in an indented try: body and provide an aligned except ExceptionType: body for its recovery action.
On a matching exception, remaining operations in the try body are skipped and the handler runs; without an exception the handler is skipped.
An unmatched exception is passed to an outer handler, or stops execution if none is found.
Use except ValueError: to handle an invalid numeric conversion from entered text.

briefs.learning_objective: Bring code from another module into the current file using import.

required_facts.statement: import module binds the module name; use module.member to access its functionality.
from module import member binds that member directly in the importing namespace.
After import math, a call such as math.cos(value) accesses a math function.

briefs.learning_objective: Write idiomatic, PEP 8-compliant Python for readability (naming, spacing, line length).

required_facts.statement: Use four spaces per block indentation level.
Use lowercase function and variable names, separating words with underscores when this improves readability.
Avoid extra spaces immediately inside parentheses, brackets or braces, before commas or colons, and between a function name and its call parentheses.
Use a single space on either side of assignment and comparison operators, while grouping arithmetic spacing to reflect priority.
PEP 8 recommends limiting code lines to 79 characters and flowing comments or docstrings to 72 characters.

briefs.learning_objective: Iterate a known, finite number of times over a sequence using a for loop.

required_facts.statement: Write for item in sequence: followed by an indented body to process successive sequence items in their order.
Initialize total = 0 before the loop, then assign total = total + item inside the loop to accumulate the numeric items.

briefs.learning_objective: Alter normal loop iteration using break (exit early) and continue (skip to the next iteration).

required_facts.statement: break exits the innermost enclosing for or while loop.
continue skips the rest of the current loop body and proceeds to the next iteration.
Place break or continue in a conditional inside the loop so it applies only when its condition holds.

briefs.learning_objective: Iterate over the elements of Python's core data structures (lists, dicts, sets, tuples) uniformly.

required_facts.statement: Use for item in collection: with an indented body to visit successive elements.
Lists and tuples are ordered sequences.
Sets are unordered, so their traversal is not positional sequence traversal.
Iterating a dictionary directly visits its keys.
Use for key, value in mapping.items(): to visit dictionary key-value pairs together.

briefs.learning_objective: Build a new list or dict in one expression using comprehension syntax.

required_facts.statement: [expression for item in iterable if condition] builds a new list by evaluating expression for the items that pass the optional condition.
{key_expression: value_expression for item in iterable} builds a dictionary from computed keys and values; an if clause can filter the items.

briefs.learning_objective: Read and write text and CSV files from Python using open() and the csv module.

required_facts.statement: open(path, mode) returns a file object; r reads and w writes, replacing existing contents.
Use with open(path, mode) as f: followed by an indented body so that f is closed after use.
f.read() reads the remaining contents; f.write(text) writes text through a text-mode file object.
Without managed opening, call f.close() when finished.
Open a CSV file with newline="" for the CSV reader.
csv.DictReader(f) produces row dictionaries using the first row as keys by default, excluding that header row from results; list(csv.DictReader(f)) collects those rows.

briefs.learning_objective: Choose a built-in collection for a storage requirement.

required_facts.statement: A list is a mutable sequence, suitable for ordered positional access with updates.
A tuple is an immutable sequence, suitable for a fixed ordered group of values.
A set stores distinct hashable values without sequence positions and supports membership tests and set operations.
A dictionary maps hashable keys to values, supports updates and preserves insertion order; use it for lookup by key rather than by sequence position.

briefs.learning_objective: Implement a simple text-based console interaction.

required_facts.statement: input(prompt) displays an optional prompt and returns entered text without its trailing newline.
print(value1, value2, ...) displays values separated by a space by default and ends with a newline; sep and end customize those delimiters.

briefs.learning_objective: Iterate over values together with their positions using enumerate.

required_facts.statement: enumerate(sequence, start=0) supplies pairs of a counter and the corresponding element; the counter starts at zero by default.
Use for position, value in enumerate(sequence, start=1): with an indented body to number entries from one without updating a manual counter.

briefs.learning_objective: Account for floating-point approximation in numeric comparisons.

required_facts.statement: Many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly as binary floating-point values.
math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=..., abs_tol=...) compares values using relative and absolute tolerances rather than exact equality.
The default relative tolerance is 1e-9 and absolute tolerance is 0.0; comparison to zero requires an appropriate positive absolute tolerance when nonzero differences should count as close.

briefs.learning_objective: Use indentation to express Python block structure.

required_facts.statement: A compound statement’s header ends with a colon and its multi-line suite is an indented block; nested suites require deeper indentation.
Indentation determines statement grouping; dedenting ends a deeper group, and inconsistent indentation can be invalid.
Use four spaces for each indentation level when repairing block structure.

briefs.learning_objective: Select math functions for a numeric calculation.

required_facts.statement: After import math, math.sqrt(x) returns the square root of x.
math functions operate on real rather than complex values; an invalid operation such as sqrt(-1.0) raises ValueError.

briefs.learning_objective: Access and update values in nested collections.

required_facts.statement: A collection can contain other collections; successive indices and keys select progressively nested values.
Assign to the final selected list index or dictionary key to update that nested value.

briefs.learning_objective: Write and trace nested loops.

required_facts.statement: Place an indented inner for loop in an outer for loop to traverse the inner collection for each outer item.
For nested rows, for row in rows: with a nested for cell in row: visits each row’s cells before proceeding to the next row.

briefs.learning_objective: Use range for bounded integer iteration.

required_facts.statement: range(stop) starts at zero with step one; range(start, stop, step) uses the specified start and nonzero step.
The stop value is excluded; a positive step continues below stop and a negative step continues above stop.
Use for index in range(start, stop, 2): to traverse every second integer position in an increasing interval.

briefs.learning_objective: Run a saved Python script with the intended interpreter.

required_facts.statement: Invoke an explicitly chosen Python executable with a script path as its argument to execute the script.
print sends script output to the standard output stream by default.
A zero process exit status indicates successful termination and a nonzero status abnormal termination; sys.exit(status) requests that status.

briefs.learning_objective: Distinguish statements from expressions during Python evaluation.

required_facts.statement: An expression statement evaluates an expression; in interactive mode its non-None value is displayed.
An assignment evaluates its right-hand expression before binding the resulting value to its target.
Python evaluates expressions from left to right; operator precedence and parentheses determine how constituent operations group.

briefs.learning_objective: Write source comments that explain non-obvious intent.

required_facts.statement: A # outside a string starts a comment extending to the physical line’s end; comments are ignored by syntax.
Keep comments accurate when code changes, because a comment contradicting code is worse than no comment.
Use inline comments sparingly and explain a useful reason rather than restating an obvious operation.

briefs.learning_objective: Use the interactive interpreter to investigate small expressions.

required_facts.statement: Starting the interpreter without a script enters interactive mode, with >>> for a new command and ... for continuation.
Entering an expression displays its result, and a variable assigned in the session can be used by later expressions.
Type commands without copying the prompt characters; lines without prompts in tutorial examples are output.

briefs.learning_objective: Explain how Python executes source in a selected runtime.

required_facts.statement: Source can be compiled to a code object; invalid source syntax raises SyntaxError.
In CPython, the compiler produces bytecode used by the interpreter; bytecode is an implementation detail, not a cross-implementation guarantee.
Top-level module statements execute when the module is first imported or when its file is executed as a script.
At runtime, an assignment evaluates its expression using current values and binds the result to its target.

briefs.learning_objective: Continue a Python expression across lines safely.

required_facts.statement: Expressions inside parentheses, square brackets or braces may span physical lines without backslashes.
Keep the delimiters and expression intact when splitting a long call across lines; continuation indentation does not determine block grouping.
Align continuation arguments with the opening delimiter or use a hanging indent.

briefs.learning_objective: Transform and split text using string methods.

required_facts.statement: text.strip() returns text with leading and trailing whitespace removed; it does not remove interior whitespace.
The optional chars argument to strip is a set of removable characters, not a literal prefix or suffix.
text.lower() returns a copy with cased characters converted to lowercase.
text.split(separator) separates on that delimiter and preserves empty fields between repeated delimiters.
text.split() without a separator splits on runs of whitespace and omits leading and trailing empty fields.

briefs.learning_objective: Distinguish syntax errors from runtime failures.

required_facts.statement: Syntax errors occur while parsing source; the error report identifies the line and location where the parser detected invalid syntax.
Syntactically valid code can raise an exception during execution; its error message identifies the exception type and explanation.
Invalid syntax prevents the source from compiling to an executable code object, so repair the syntax before tracing that source’s runtime behavior.

briefs.learning_objective: Use Python truth-value rules in conditions.

required_facts.statement: False, None, numeric zero and empty built-in strings and collections have false truth values; nonzero numbers and nonempty built-in strings and collections have true truth values.
Use if collection: for a nonempty guard or if not collection: for an empty guard; truth testing does not require equality to True.

briefs.learning_objective: Check for the absence sentinel None using identity.

required_facts.statement: None is the singleton object commonly used to represent absence of a value.
is tests whether operands are the same object and is not tests whether they are different objects.
Use value is None or value is not None to test absence rather than a truth test that would also reject a legitimate zero or empty value.

briefs.learning_objective: Encode and decode between Unicode strings and bytes.

required_facts.statement: str contains Unicode text, distinct from binary bytes.
text.encode("utf-8") produces bytes using UTF-8.
payload.decode("utf-8") produces text from UTF-8 bytes; the decoding encoding must match the encoded data to recover that text.
A decoding failure raises UnicodeDecodeError when the supplied bytes are not valid for the chosen decoding.

briefs.learning_objective: Traverse corresponding values from parallel iterables using zip.

required_facts.statement: zip(left, right) pairs corresponding elements into tuples for parallel traversal.
Use for left_item, right_item in zip(left, right): to process each pair in an indented body.
By default zip stops at the shortest input, omitting unmatched trailing values from longer inputs.

briefs.learning_objective: Avoid unintended collection mutation through aliases and shallow copies.

required_facts.statement: Assignment can bind multiple names to the same object rather than copying it; mutating a shared list or dictionary can be visible through other names and to a function’s caller.
items.copy() or items[:] creates a shallow copy of a list, allowing independent changes to that list’s top-level items.
A shallow copy still contains references to the original elements, so a nested mutable element can remain shared.

briefs.learning_objective: Count repeated values with collections.Counter.

required_facts.statement: After from collections import Counter, Counter(items) counts occurrences of hashable elements in a mapping from elements to counts.
counts.most_common(1) returns a list with the most frequent element and its count, or an empty list for an empty counter.
most_common orders pairs by descending count, with ties ordered by first encounter; access the first returned pair only if the result is nonempty.

briefs.learning_objective: Inspect Python state using temporary diagnostic output.

required_facts.statement: print(label, value) displays a label and a value to reveal the state at that execution point.
repr(value) returns a printable representation that can expose details obscured by ordinary string display.
Place diagnostic output after the binding or before the operation being investigated to observe that current value; removing the print call removes that diagnostic output.

briefs.learning_objective: Document a reusable Python interface with a docstring.

required_facts.statement: Document public functions, modules, classes and methods with docstrings.
Place a string literal first in a function body to provide its docstring, with a concise purpose summary and additional calling-convention details after a blank line.
Document the function’s arguments, return values and applicable exceptions as part of its interface.
help(function) displays documentation for the function, including its docstring and signature.

briefs.learning_objective: Classify Python exception types by their position in the exception hierarchy.

required_facts.statement: BaseException is the root of the built-in exception hierarchy, and Exception is its subclass for ordinary application failures.
ValueError and OSError are subclasses of Exception, and FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError.
KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit and GeneratorExit are directly under BaseException rather than under Exception.

briefs.learning_objective: Trace exception propagation through function calls.

required_facts.statement: A raised exception skips the remaining operations in its current try body and searches for a matching handler.
Handler matching accepts an exception of the named class or a subclass; handlers are examined in their written order.
If no local handler matches, the exception propagates through the callers to an outer handler, or becomes unhandled if none matches.
When a handler recovers, execution continues after its try/except statement, not at the failed operation.

briefs.learning_objective: Guarantee cleanup with finally.

required_facts.statement: Place release operations in an aligned finally: body following try: to run them when leaving the protected operation.
finally executes on normal completion, on an exception and on a return from the try body.
An unhandled exception is re-raised after finally completes normally; a return from finally can replace a pending return or suppress a pending exception.

briefs.learning_objective: Pass functions as callback values.

required_facts.statement: A function definition creates a function object bound to its name; the bare name refers to the function and name(arguments) calls it.
Functions can be passed where a function object is required.
A callable can be stored and invoked later.
A receiving helper can call a supplied function parameter using parameter(value), rather than passing the result of an earlier call.

briefs.learning_objective: Capture enclosing function state in a closure.

required_facts.statement: A nested function can resolve a free name in an enclosing function scope; each call has its own local bindings.
A returned nested function can use enclosing values after its creating call has finished.
Declare nonlocal name in a nested function to rebind an existing name in the nearest enclosing function scope.
A stateful factory can bind state in its body and return a nested function that reads and rebinds that state with nonlocal.

briefs.learning_objective: Construct and resolve filesystem paths using pathlib.

required_facts.statement: from pathlib import Path provides concrete paths using the platform’s path conventions.
base / "child" constructs a child path; an absolute right operand replaces the previous path rather than remaining underneath it.
Relative paths are interpreted against the current working directory; choosing an explicit base directory avoids relying on an unintended working directory.

briefs.learning_objective: Raise a meaningful exception for an invalid operation.

required_facts.statement: Use raise ExceptionType(message) to signal a particular failure with explanatory context.
ValueError indicates an argument of an appropriate type but an inappropriate value, apart from cases with a more precise exception.
Use specific exceptions to permit precise handling.

briefs.learning_objective: Locate Python failures from tracebacks.

required_facts.statement: The final line of an exception report gives the exception type and message.
The traceback’s preceding frames give source locations and the calling context where the exception occurred.
Traceback frames in a call chain lead down to the most recent failing operation; use its displayed file, line and statement to locate the immediate cause.

briefs.learning_objective: Inspect Python execution using breakpoints and stepping.

required_facts.statement: breakpoint() enters the debugger at the call site; by default it invokes pdb.set_trace().
In pdb, p expression prints an expression’s value, and l lists nearby source lines.
n executes the next line without stepping into a called function, s steps into calls, and c continues until another breakpoint or termination.
Use b line_number to set a breakpoint and inspect the values controlling a suspect branch when execution pauses there.

briefs.learning_objective: Avoid shared mutable function defaults.

required_facts.statement: Default argument values are evaluated once at definition time, so a mutable default can retain modifications across calls.
Use a None default and an if parameter is None: branch that creates a new list or dictionary in the function body to obtain fresh per-call state.

briefs.learning_objective: Order iterable values using a key function.

required_facts.statement: sorted(records, key=function) returns a new sorted list and uses function(record) as each record’s comparison key.
sorted does not mutate the original list; reverse=True reverses the ordering.
Sorting is stable: items with equal keys retain their original relative order.
str.lower can provide a lowercase text key for case-normalized ordering.

briefs.learning_objective: Write a small anonymous callable using lambda.

required_facts.statement: lambda parameters: expression creates an anonymous function whose result is the single expression’s value.
A lambda is restricted to one expression and can be passed as key=lambda item: expression to sorting.

briefs.learning_objective: Select and order specific Python exception handlers.

required_facts.statement: An except handler matches its named exception class and subclasses; the first matching handler runs.
Order subclass-specific handlers before broader parent handlers so the specific recovery remains reachable.
FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError, so except FileNotFoundError: must precede except OSError: when their recovery actions differ.

briefs.learning_objective: Diagnose whether a Python failure comes from invalid input, an implementation defect or an external operational problem.

required_facts.statement: ValueError can identify an unsuitable value such as malformed numeric input; reject or request correction of an input that violates the stated value contract.
NameError means a local or global name cannot be found; a misspelled implementation name calls for code correction rather than rejection of the supplied input.
PermissionError reports inadequate access rights for a filesystem operation; report the access failure rather than assuming the supplied path or implementation is inherently wrong.

briefs.learning_objective: Bind variable arguments using *args and **kwargs.

required_facts.statement: In a function definition, *args collects remaining positional arguments into a tuple.
In a function definition, **kwargs collects additional keyword arguments into a dictionary; a parameter may not receive two values in a call.
In a call, *args expands a sequence into positional arguments and **kwargs expands a dictionary into keyword arguments.
A forwarding wrapper can define def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): and return target(*args, **kwargs), avoiding additional arguments that duplicate a supplied binding.

briefs.learning_objective: Define classes and create ordinary instances.

required_facts.statement: class ClassName: followed by an indented body creates a class object; pass can supply an empty body.
Calling an ordinary class with ClassName() creates a new instance; two such calls create distinct instances.
is tests object identity, so first is second distinguishes shared identity from two separate instances.

briefs.learning_objective: Select Python file modes without unintended data loss.

required_facts.statement: open(path, "r") reads an existing file; r is the default mode.
open(path, "w") writes and truncates an existing file, or creates a new file.
open(path, "a") appends to an existing file or creates it.
open(path, "x") exclusively creates a new file and fails if it exists.
Handle FileExistsError when exclusive creation finds an existing destination, rather than changing to a truncating mode unintentionally.

briefs.learning_objective: Initialize per-instance state with __init__.

required_facts.statement: If a class defines __init__, instantiation automatically invokes it on the new instance and passes the constructor arguments.
Define def __init__(self, first, second): in the class and assign self.first = first and self.second = second to initialize those instance attributes.
__init__ initializes the created instance rather than returning a replacement object.

briefs.learning_objective: Implement instance behavior using self.

required_facts.statement: An instance method receives the target instance as its first argument, conventionally named self.
Define def method(self, argument): inside the class and use self.attribute to read or reassign that instance’s state.
instance.method(value) passes instance implicitly as self and value as the next argument.

briefs.learning_objective: Choose the method binding appropriate to an object's operation.

required_facts.statement: An instance method receives the instance as its implicit first argument and can use that instance’s state.
Put @classmethod above def method(cls, ...): to receive the class as the implicit first argument; return cls(arguments) to construct an instance in an alternative constructor.
Put @staticmethod above def method(...): for an operation with no implicit instance or class argument.

briefs.learning_objective: Combine collaborating objects through composition.

required_facts.statement: Instance data attributes can hold collaborator objects.
Store a collaborator as self.collaborator and invoke self.collaborator.method(arguments) from an instance method to delegate work to that object.

briefs.learning_objective: Apply Python conventions for non-public object state.

required_facts.statement: A leading underscore conventionally marks a non-public implementation name; it does not enforce access protection.
Python does not provide truly inaccessible private instance attributes through this naming convention.
Public attributes form the interface expected to be used by clients; keep implementation details non-public with a leading underscore.
Expose a public method that operates on the receiving instance’s supporting attributes instead of requiring callers to manage that state directly.

briefs.learning_objective: Extend inherited behavior using super().

required_facts.statement: Define class Derived(Base): to inherit from Base; an overridden method replaces the inherited method for ordinary lookup on Derived instances.
Inside an ordinary derived instance method, super().method(arguments) delegates lookup to the next class in method resolution order.
In a derived __init__, call super().__init__(arguments) to run inherited initialization before adding derived initialization where required.

briefs.learning_objective: Define an application-specific exception type.

required_facts.statement: Define an application-specific exception as a class derived from Exception, using class CustomError(Exception): with an indented pass body.
raise CustomError(message) signals that custom failure; except CustomError: handles it at a surrounding boundary.

briefs.learning_objective: Distinguish instance state from shared class attributes.

required_facts.statement: Class variables hold attributes shared by instances, while instance variables hold data unique to an instance.
A mutable list assigned in the class body is shared unless shadowed by an instance attribute.
Assign self.items = [] in __init__ to create a separate list for each instance rather than mutating a shared class list.

briefs.learning_objective: Serialize and deserialize supported Python data using the json module.

required_facts.statement: json.dumps(value) serializes supported Python values to a JSON str.
json.loads(text) deserializes a JSON string into Python values.
Default conversions support dictionaries, lists, tuples, strings, numeric values, booleans and None; lists and tuples both encode as arrays, which decode as lists.
JSON object keys are strings, so non-string dictionary keys need not retain their original Python types on a round trip.

briefs.learning_objective: Inspect Python object types and attributes.

required_facts.statement: type(object) returns the object’s type.
isinstance(object, Class) checks whether the object is an instance of that class or one of its subclasses.
dir(object) attempts to list relevant attribute names, but is not guaranteed to be complete.
getattr(object, name) retrieves a named attribute, with an optional fallback if it is absent.
Attribute names beginning with an underscore conventionally signal internal use rather than a public interface.

briefs.learning_objective: Perform filesystem operations using pathlib.

required_facts.statement: directory.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) creates the directory and missing parents, allowing an existing directory; both options default to False.
directory.iterdir() traverses its immediate entries in arbitrary order.
source.rename(target) renames or moves the entry to target; a relative target is resolved against the current working directory, not against source’s parent.
rename can silently replace an existing target file on Unix when permitted, while Windows raises FileExistsError for an existing target.
Construct the destination as directory / filename to target the selected output directory rather than relying on a bare relative filename.

briefs.learning_objective: Define readable object representations using special methods.

required_facts.statement: Define def __repr__(self): returning a str for an information-rich, unambiguous representation used by repr and interactive inspection.
Define def __str__(self): returning a str for a convenient user-facing representation used by str and print.
If __str__ is not defined, the default representation uses __repr__.

briefs.learning_objective: Specify the encoding contract for text-file access.

required_facts.statement: Use open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") to decode UTF-8 text and open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") to encode written text explicitly.
The encoding argument specifies the text encoding; the selected encoding must match the file’s bytes for correct decoding.
A UnicodeDecodeError indicates a decoding failure, which can arise when the file’s bytes are invalid for the selected encoding.

briefs.learning_objective: Handle expected file and parsing failures at a Python I/O boundary.

required_facts.statement: FileNotFoundError indicates that the requested file or directory does not exist; handle it separately from content problems.
UnicodeDecodeError indicates failure to decode the content using the selected encoding.
csv.Error reports errors detected by the CSV parser; except csv.Error: can provide a parsing-failure response.

DictReader fills missing fields with restval, defaulting to None, and places excess fields under restkey, defaulting to None; validate required row fields explicitly rather than assuming malformed row lengths raise csv.Error.
Wrap the import at a boundary with specific exception handlers for missing files, decoding and parser failures, and report each according to its cause.

briefs.learning_objective: Manage resource lifetimes using with.

required_facts.statement: Use with context_expression as resource: followed by an indented body; the context manager enters before the body and exits after it.
Once entry succeeds, the exit method runs whether the body completes normally or raises an exception; a context manager may suppress an exception.
For with open(path) as f:, leaving the body closes the file, including when the body raises.

briefs.learning_objective: Read and write bytes through binary file streams.

required_facts.statement: The b mode selects binary I/O: open(path, "rb") reads bytes and open(path, "wb") writes bytes rather than str.
wb creates or truncates the destination file.
Read a binary payload with source.read() and write that bytes value with destination.write(payload) to copy it without text decoding.
Use managed opening with with to close both files after the copy.

briefs.learning_objective: Calculate date and time differences with datetime.

required_facts.statement: datetime.strptime(text, format) parses text according to an explicit format, and .date() obtains its calendar date.
Use %Y-%m-%d for a year-month-day numeric date.
Subtracting one date from another returns a timedelta representing their difference.
For calendar dates, (later_date - earlier_date).days gives their signed day difference.

optional_enrichment.statement: Subtract datetime values only with compatible timezone awareness: two naive values or two aware values; mixing naive and aware values raises TypeError.

briefs.learning_objective: Extract reusable code into a local Python module.

required_facts.statement: A module is a file of Python definitions and statements, with a .py suffix; its filename without that suffix supplies the module name.
Move a shared helper definition into a sibling module, then import module and call module.helper(arguments), or use from module import helper.
In ordinary script invocation, the script’s directory is included in the module search path, permitting sibling-module imports.

briefs.learning_objective: Organize local importable Python packages.

required_facts.statement: A regular package groups modules in a directory containing __init__.py; that file may be empty.
Use import package.module and package.module.helper(arguments), or from package.module import helper, to access a packaged helper.

briefs.learning_objective: Report program events using logging.

required_facts.statement: After import logging, logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) obtains a logger named for the module.

DEBUG is for detailed diagnostics, INFO for expected progress, WARNING for an unexpected condition while operation continues, ERROR for inability to perform a function, and CRITICAL for a serious failure.
Emit events with logger.debug(message) or logger.info(message), choosing a method corresponding to the desired level.
Configure application logging with logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) to include INFO and higher events; the default root threshold is WARNING.
Propagation normally passes events to ancestor handlers; attaching handlers to both a logger and its ancestors can duplicate output, so ordinarily configure a handler at one suitable ancestor.

briefs.learning_objective: Separate importable definitions from script-only execution.

required_facts.statement: A module executed as the main script has __name__ equal to "__main__"; an imported module has its module name instead.
Put command-interface actions under if __name__ == "__main__": so importing the module does not execute those actions.
Keep reusable helper definitions outside that guarded command-interface body so importers can use them.

briefs.learning_objective: Parse a script's command-line interface with argparse.

required_facts.statement: After import argparse, create parser = argparse.ArgumentParser() to define a command interface.
parser.add_argument("input_path") declares a required positional value, while a name starting with -- declares an option.
parser.add_argument("--verbose", action="store_true") creates a boolean flag that defaults to False and becomes True when present.
args = parser.parse_args() parses the command line into attributes such as args.input_path and args.verbose.
By default invalid arguments produce an error message and exit status 2; missing required arguments are invalid.

briefs.learning_objective: Diagnose Python module discovery and name shadowing.

required_facts.statement: After checking built-in modules, an ordinary import searches sys.path for the named module; the script directory normally comes before standard-library directories.
A local file with the same name as a standard-library module can shadow that module; rename the conflicting local file to remove that ambiguity.
Inspect sys.path to see the search locations used by the interpreter.
Inspect module.__file__ to locate a file-backed imported module.

briefs.learning_objective: Read environment-variable configuration with os.environ.

required_facts.statement: os.environ maps process environment names to string values.
os.environ.get("SETTING", fallback) returns the configured string or fallback if the name is absent; without a fallback it returns None for absence.
For a required setting, check absence explicitly or use bracket lookup, which raises KeyError for a missing key; report missing configuration instead of proceeding with an unintended value.

briefs.learning_objective: Choose random or secrets according to the use of randomness.

required_facts.statement: random is designed for modelling and simulation, while secrets provides cryptographically strong randomness for security-sensitive values.
random.seed(seed) initializes the pseudo-random generator; reuse a seed to reproduce a sequence under the documented reproducibility conditions.
random.random() returns a floating-point value in the half-open interval from 0.0 to 1.0.
secrets.token_hex(nbytes) generates a random hexadecimal token for security-sensitive use.

briefs.learning_objective: Recognize simple text patterns using re.

required_facts.statement: A regular expression describes a text pattern; [...] selects one character from a set, ranges such as A-Z select a range, and * allows zero or more repetitions.
Concatenated pattern elements match in sequence; a raw string literal such as r"..." avoids Python string-escape processing of pattern backslashes.
re.fullmatch(pattern, text) returns a Match if the whole text matches and None otherwise; test is not None for successful validation.
re.match checks at the beginning, while re.search looks for a match anywhere; neither requires the entire text to match.

briefs.learning_objective: Inspect interpreter runtime information using sys.

required_facts.statement: sys.executable gives the running interpreter’s executable path when available; it may be an empty string or None if Python cannot retrieve it.
sys.version gives the interpreter version plus build and compiler information.
After import sys, print(sys.executable) and print(sys.version) display which runtime is actually executing the code.

briefs.learning_objective: Create and use an isolated Python virtual environment.

required_facts.statement: Run the selected Python executable with -m venv .venv to create a project environment, containing bin/python on POSIX or Scripts/python.exe on Windows.
Activation changes command lookup to the environment’s executable, but activation is not required when invoking that executable by its full path.
sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix identifies an interpreter running in a virtual environment.
Run the environment’s Python with -m pip list to inspect its installed packages.
Virtual environments are isolated from base-environment packages by default.

briefs.learning_objective: Select and verify the interpreter used for a Python project.

required_facts.statement: Inspect sys.executable in the executed program to identify its actual interpreter, rather than relying on an environment label.
A venv supplies its interpreter at bin/python on POSIX or Scripts/python.exe on Windows.
Configure an execution tool to invoke the intended venv executable explicitly when command lookup selects the wrong Python; activation is not required for explicit executable invocation.
Check sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix and the executable path again after changing the selected runtime.

briefs.learning_objective: Install dependencies using the intended Python environment's pip.

required_facts.statement: Invoke the intended environment’s interpreter with -m pip install package_name to install that distribution into that interpreter’s environment.
Use -m pip show package_name or -m pip list through the same interpreter to inspect the installation.
Import the package’s documented import name using the same interpreter to verify it is usable there.
A distribution package installed by pip is not necessarily named the same as the import package used in Python code.

briefs.learning_objective: Recreate an environment's dependencies from a requirements file.

required_facts.statement: A requirements file lists dependencies, and package_name==version pins a specific version.
Invoke the fresh environment’s Python with -m pip install -r requirements.txt to install the listed requirements.
Use the same interpreter’s -m pip list to inspect installed versions.
Check required imports in the recreated interpreter rather than assuming an installation report proves each module is importable.

briefs.learning_objective: Use assert to express development-only invariants.

required_facts.statement: assert condition, message raises AssertionError when the condition is false in normal debugging execution.
Python can omit assert statements when optimization is requested with -O, so an assertion must not replace input checks required in production.
Use an explicit conditional and raise for required runtime validation rather than relying on a removable debugging assertion.

briefs.learning_objective: Distinguish iterables from iterators.

required_facts.statement: An iterable supplies an iterator via iter(value); an iterator supplies successive values via next(iterator) and signals exhaustion with StopIteration.
Separate iter(list_value) calls produce separate traversal state, while the list stores the reusable items.
Calling iter on an iterator returns that same iterator rather than a new independent traversal.
next(iterator, default) returns default when the iterator is exhausted instead of raising StopIteration.

briefs.learning_objective: Produce lazy values with yield.

required_facts.statement: A function containing yield creates a generator iterator when called; advancing it runs until the next yield.
yield value supplies one item and suspends execution, retaining local state until the next advance.
Write a for loop and a condition inside a generator function, yielding each accepted item; reaching the function’s end terminates iteration.

briefs.learning_objective: Write generator expressions for lazy transformations.

required_facts.statement: (expression for item in iterable if condition) defines a generator that transforms accepted items lazily; the filtering if clause is optional.
The leftmost iterable expression is evaluated immediately, while item transformations and filtering happen during iteration.
Pass a generator expression as the sole argument to sum to total transformed values without creating an intermediate list.

briefs.learning_objective: Account for iterator consumption and exhaustion.

required_facts.statement: Each next(iterator) consumes the next available item; a traversal or consumer sees only the remaining items.
Once an iterator raises StopIteration, it must continue to do so on subsequent calls.
iter(iterator) returns the same iterator and does not reset it.
For another pass over a reusable collection, obtain a fresh iterator from that collection rather than reusing its exhausted iterator.

briefs.learning_objective: Choose eager or lazy processing for an iterable workload.

required_facts.statement: list(iterable) materializes its remaining items into a list that can be traversed repeatedly.
Generator expressions compute values as consumed and tend to use less memory than equivalent list comprehensions.
For a one-pass total, sum(expression for item in iterable) avoids constructing an intermediate transformed list.
An iterator is consumed as it advances and stays exhausted after completion, so repeated reuse may require a stored collection or a new source traversal.

briefs.learning_objective: Chain iterable inputs lazily using itertools.chain.

required_facts.statement: After from itertools import chain, chain(first, second) traverses each input in order, exhausting the first before moving to the second, without first concatenating them into a list.
sum(chain(first, second)) totals numeric items from the combined traversal.

briefs.learning_objective: Choose a readable iterable transformation idiom.

required_facts.statement: map(function, iterable) lazily applies a callable to successive items and yields the results.
filter(predicate, iterable) lazily yields items for which the predicate is true; filter(None, iterable) keeps truthy items.
filter(predicate, iterable) corresponds to (item for item in iterable if predicate(item)).

[function(item) for item in iterable if predicate(item)] makes a materialized transform-and-filter list and can replace a map/filter composition when that form communicates the computation more clearly.
Use a parenthesized generator expression instead of a list comprehension when preserving lazy traversal is required.

briefs.learning_objective: Express supplied checks in Python unittest.TestCase syntax.

required_facts.statement: After import unittest, define class Tests(unittest.TestCase): with methods named test_* to express individual supplied checks.
Use self.assertEqual(actual, expected) for equality and self.assertTrue(condition) for a required true condition.
Use with self.assertRaises(ExceptionType): around the supplied failing operation to check that it raises the expected exception.

briefs.learning_objective: Run Python unittest discovery and interpret runner outcomes.

required_facts.statement: python -m unittest test_module runs a named test module, and python -m unittest discover invokes test discovery.
Discovery defaults to the current directory and test*.py filenames; -s selects a starting directory and -p selects a filename pattern.
A failure is an unsuccessful assertion check; the runner report identifies the test and traceback for the failed assertion.
An error is an unexpected exception during a test rather than an explicitly failed assertion.
The reported test count records how many tests ran; a count of zero supplies no executed checks of the helper’s behavior.

briefs.learning_objective: Implement isolated unittest fixtures with setup and cleanup hooks.

required_facts.statement: Define setUp(self) to initialize fresh per-test state before each test method; an error in setUp prevents that test method from running.
tearDown(self) runs after a test when setUp succeeded, including when the test failed.
self.addCleanup(function, *args, **kwargs) registers cleanup that runs after tearDown, or after a failed setUp; registered actions run in reverse registration order.
Register the release callable after acquiring the supplied test resource and store mutable test data on self in setUp rather than in shared class attributes.

briefs.learning_objective: Explain generated code in terms of the stated requirements.

required_facts.statement: Trace each supplied input through the conditions to its actual return; a path reaching the end of a function without a return produces None.
Track each assignment and selected branch in order to determine the actual data and control flow for valid and invalid inputs.
Code from a virtual assistant can be mistaken, so check its behavior rather than treating its generated form as proof of correctness.

briefs.learning_objective: Check generated Python code for destructive filesystem behavior.

required_facts.statement: Opening a file in w mode truncates existing content; inspect generated mode choices to identify an unintended overwrite.
Path.unlink() removes the file or symbolic link at that path; remove an unintended unlink call instead of executing it.
Path.rename(target) moves an entry and can replace an existing file on Unix; inspect the actual source and destination paths.

An absolute child path replaces a preceding base path, and a relative rename target is interpreted against the working directory; trace these path rules to check the actual destination before execution.

briefs.learning_objective: Reject unsafe execution of untrusted input in generated Python code.

required_facts.statement: eval evaluates a Python expression and can execute arbitrary code, so it must not be used to process untrusted text.
exec executes Python code supplied as text or a code object and is unsafe for untrusted instructions.
Invoking a shell makes quoting and metacharacters a security responsibility; inspect shell=True and untrusted command construction for injection risk.
Replace execution-based parsing with a parser matching the expected data, such as int or float for numeric text and json.loads for JSON, with explicit validation and handling of malformed input.
Non-executing parsing is not unlimited resource safety: impose input-size limits for untrusted JSON because malicious input can consume substantial CPU and memory.

briefs.learning_objective: Check generated Python API claims in authoritative documentation.

required_facts.statement: An official API entry such as sorted documents its signature, keyword-only options and returned value; compare a generated call’s name, arguments and expected result to those documented elements.
Virtual assistants can make mistakes even about Python, so their plausible API claims need checking.
help(object) displays documentation for an available object, supporting inspection of its actual interface in the selected runtime.
Check the executing interpreter’s version when comparing an API claim to version-specific documentation.

briefs.learning_objective: Verify suggested dependencies before installation.

required_facts.statement: pip installs from the Python Package Index by default; browse that index to check the actual named distribution rather than installing an unchecked suggestion.
An installable distribution package and an import package need not have the same name; confirm the distribution name from the project’s installation documentation.
An --index-url changes the package index used for installation; inspect a proposed install command’s source as well as its name.
The Python standard library supplies modules for many common tasks; check whether documented standard-library functionality already meets the requirement before adding a third-party dependency.
Assistant output can contain mistakes; withhold installation of a dependency suggestion whose identity and documented use cannot be verified.

briefs.learning_objective: Decide whether generated Python code is acceptable using evidence.

required_facts.statement: Generated code can be wrong; test code obtained from a virtual assistant rather than accepting it solely because it was generated.
Use the supplied failed assertions and unexpected exceptions to identify behavior requiring correction; these results do not support accepting the helper unchanged.

Compare traced returns and supplied test expectations with the required behavior; record acceptance only for behavior supported by that evidence, and record correction when a mismatch can be addressed.
Reject execution of a proposed implementation that evaluates untrusted input or truncates a file contrary to the requirements until those unsafe operations are removed or corrected.
